name: New South Wales Pidgin
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.source_named: Troy, Jakelin. 1994. Melaleuka: a history and description of New South Wales Pidgin. PhD thesis, ANU (includes phonology; PDF not retrieved)

sources.citation: Troy, Jakelin Fleur. 1994. Melaleuka: a history and description of New South Wales Pidgin. PhD thesis, ANU. Volume 2 (Appendices 1-22: data corpora, wordlist, phonological comparison), pp. 502-800.
sources.note: Appendix 22 ('Comparison of Dawson's data with the phonological systems of Kattang and Thangatti', pp. 790-792) treats plosives, fricatives, affricates, sibilants and vowels only; no stress. Appendix 21 wordlist does not mark stress. The only stress mention is a quoted 1865 observer (Lucy Edgar, Merri Creek near Melbourne) in Appendix 20 item 1, p. 680 (PDF page 180): speakers 'laid great stress on the vowel sounds... potatoe, which they rendered po-ta-to, laying the utmost stress on the first and last syllables' - an impressionistic remark on the pronunciation of English words, not a stress…

sources.citation: O'Shannessy, Carmel, Denise Angelo & Jane Simpson. 2024. Toward a typology of Australian contact languages (introduction). Journal of Pidgin and Creole Languages (jpcl.00137.osh). ANU handle 1885/733809896.
sources.note: Nothing on stress; mentions only that traditional-language word structure (two-syllable minimum) motivated -im suffixation in pidgin. No description of NSW Pidgin prosody.

sources.citation: Wikipedia, 'Port Jackson Pidgin English' (article source, with bibliography citing Troy 1994, Meakins 2016, Hall 1943, Muhlhausler 1991, Simpson 2000, etc.).
sources.note: No phonology or stress content; used only to harvest the secondary bibliography.

sources.citation: Troy, Jakelin. 1990. Australian Aboriginal contact with the English language in New South Wales: 1788 to 1845. Pacific Linguistics B-103. Canberra: RSPAS, ANU. xi+156 pp.
sources.note: Each period has a '(.5) PHONOLOGY' inventory described as 'a list of the phonological innovations in English as spoken by Aborigines' (p. 38); these list segmental substitutions only. No mention of stress, accent or syllable prominence (the string 'stress' occurs only as 'stressed the resources' and in a quotation of Dixon on number).
